# Lex - Vietnamese Telex input method

The specification of the Lex program, a Vietnamese Telex input method.

## Vietnamese Telex Rules

### Literal input characters

- When any of the following characters start the word (when the word is empty), change to literal
  input from the new character position: `F`, `J`, `W`, `Z` (ignore cases), because these characters
  don't start a Vietnamese word. This rule is higher priority than diacritics and tones rules.
- When any of the following characters are added to the word, change to literal input from the new
  character position: `F`, `J`, `W` (ignore cases), because these characters don't appear in formal
  Vietnamese spelling. `Z` exists in Vietnamese word such as _Dzũng_, _Hồ Dzếnh_... This rule is
  lower priority than diacritics and tones rules.
- Literal input remains until the new word.
- When the user backspaces pass before the literal point, we switch to Vietnamese input again.

### Diacritics

Diacritics let a character have many variant. We only focus on character diacritics in this section.
Tones have a separate section.

#### Empty

- Any literal alphabet character has empty diacritic by default.
- Only a specific number of characters have other diacritic and it must follow the rules for those
  characters.

#### Circumflex

- Valid for: `A` (Â), `E` (Ê), `O` (Ô) and their lower cases.

#### Breve

- Valid for: `A` (Ă) and its lower case.

#### Horn

- Valid for: `O` (Ơ), `U` (Ư) and their lower cases.

#### Stroke

- Valid for: `D` (Đ) and its lower case.

#### Apply rules

- Only apply diacritic when the immediate previous character doesn't have any diacritic (empty).
- _Circumflex_, _stroke_ are triggered when user inputs the same character (ignore case) with the
  existing character when that character is valid for the applying diacritic.
  - `Aa` -> `Â`, `Ee` -> `Ê`, `Oo` -> `Ô`.
  - `Dd` -> `Đ`.
- _Breve_, _horn_ are triggered when user input `W`, `w` after the character when that character is
  valid for the applying diacritic. Otherwise, treat `W`, `w` literally.
  - `Aw` -> `Ă`.
  - `Ow` -> `Ơ`, `Uw` -> `Ư`.
- The existing character keep its case, tone.
- Treat out of scope characters as literal.

#### Override rules

- New valid diacritic can override existing valid diacritic of the same base character.
  - `Ăa` -> `Â`, `Âw` -> `Ă`.
  - `Ôw` -> `Ơ`, `Ơo` -> `Ô`.
- Only `A`, `O` have override rules because they have more than one possible character diacritic.
- Keep tone untouched.
- The existing character keep its case, tone.
- Treat out of scope characters as literal.

#### Cancel rules

- The cancellation is triggered if and only if user inputs the character (ignore case) that would
  produce the existing diacritic for the same base character of the immediate previous character.
- The existing character keeps its case, tone, but the diacritic is removed.
  - Circumflex: `Âa` -> `Aa`, `Ốo` -> `Óo`... and so on for other cases of the same kind.
  - Breve: `Ăw` -> `Aw`.
  - Horn: `Ưw` -> `Uw`... and so on for other cases of the same kind.
  - Stroke: `Đd` -> `Dd`, `đD` -> `dD`.
- The new character is literal, keeps its case, no tone.
- Switch to literal from the new character position and the following characters. Literal input
  remains until the new word.
  - Existing `Â`, input `aa`, result `Aaa`.
- When the user backspaces pass before the literal point, we switch to Vietnamese input again.

#### Auto-fill rules

- The auto-fill is only applied for `ươ` syllable immediately before the user input, when one of the
  character in the syllable is missing horn: `uơ` and `ưo`.
- Fill the missing _horn_ when the input is one of these character (ignore case): `C`, `I`, `M`,
  `N`, `P`, `T`, `U` and their lower cases.
  - Fill missing horn on `U`: `uơn` -> `ươn`.
  - Fill missing horn on `O`: `ưóp` -> `ướp`.
- The new input character is appended literally.
- Tone and case of existing characters are preserved on the original characters.

### Tones

Tones let a word have many variants, each variant has different meaning. Only the following
Vietnamese vowel could have tones: `A`, `E`, `I`, `O`, `U`, `Y` and their corresponding variants.
These vowel could take any tone.

#### Level (ngang)

- The default tone, it's the vowel without any tone mark, e.g. `A`, `Ê`, `Ơ`...and all other
  corresponding variants.
- If a vowel has tone mark other than level, use `Z`, `z` to reset the tone to level.

#### Rising (sắc)

- Example of rising tone: `Á`, `Ế`, `Ớ`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `S`, `s` to put the rising tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `As` -> `Á`, `Ês` -> `Ế`, `Ơs`
  -> `Ớ`.

#### Falling (huyền)

- Example of falling tone: `À`, `Ề`, `Ờ`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `F`, `f` to put the falling tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `Af` -> `À`, `Êf` -> `Ề`, `Ơf`
  -> `Ờ`.

#### Dipping-rising (hỏi)

- Example of dipping-rising tone: `Ả`, `Ể`, `Ở`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `R`, `r` to put the dipping-rising tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `Ar` -> `Ả`, `Êr` ->
  `Ể`, `Ơr` -> `Ở`.

#### Rising-glottalized (ngã)

- Example of rising-glottalized tone: `Ã`, `Ễ`, `Ỡ`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `X`, `x` to put the rising-glottalized tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `Ax` -> `Ã`, `Êx`
  -> `Ễ`, `Ơx` -> `Ỡ`.

#### Falling-glottalized (nặng)

- Example of falling-glottalized tone: `Ạ`, `Ệ`, `Ợ`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `J`, `j` to put the falling-glottalized tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `Aj` -> `Ạ`, `Êj`
  -> `Ệ`, `Ơj` -> `Ợ`.

#### Apply rules

- Only trigger apply tone when the buffer has existing characters. Otherwise, append the new
  character literally.
- Trigger apply tone when user inputs the trigger character for tones: `S`, `F`, `R`, `X`, `J` and
  their lower cases.
- _Scan pseudo-word_ to have the information for later steps.
- If the pseudo-word doesn't have any vowels, append new character literally.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and all of them don't have any tone (level), use _tone
  position rules_ to apply the tone for the word.
- If _tone position rules_ could not put tone to the pseudo-word, append new character literally.

#### Cancel rules

- Only trigger apply tone when the buffer has existing characters. Otherwise, append the new
  character literally.
- Trigger apply tone when user inputs the trigger character for tones: `S`, `F`, `R`, `X`, `J` and
  their lower cases.
- _Scan pseudo-word_ to have the information for later steps.
- If the pseudo-word doesn't have any vowels, handle by _apply rules_.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and has the tone (other than level) on vowels match with
  the triggered tone. Reset that tone to level. Append new character literally.
- If the new character has been appended literally, switch to literal from the new character
  position and the following characters. Literal input remains until the new word.
- When the user backspaces pass before the literal point, we switch to Vietnamese input again.

#### Reset rules

- Only trigger reset tone when the buffer has existing characters. Otherwise, append the new
  character literally.
- Trigger reset tone when user inputs the trigger character for reset: `Z`, `z`.
- _Scan pseudo-word_ to have the information for later steps.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and has tone (other than level) in one of the vowels,
  change that tone to level, keep case and diacritic.
- If the pseudo-word doesn't have any vowels, append the new character literally and remain
  Vietnamese input to continue process Vietnamese input such as `dzu + x` -> `dzũ`.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and all of them don't have any tone (level), append the
  new character literally and switch to literal from the new character position and the following
  characters. Literal input remains until the new word.
- When the user backspaces pass before the literal point, we switch to Vietnamese input again.

#### Override rules

- Only trigger override tone when the buffer has existing characters. Otherwise, append the new
  character literally.
- Trigger apply tone when user inputs the trigger character for tones: `S`, `F`, `R`, `X`, `J` and
  their lower cases.
- _Scan pseudo-word_ to have the information for later steps.
- If the pseudo-word doesn't have any vowels, handle by _apply rules_.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and has the tone (other than level) on vowels different
  from the triggered tone, reset that tone to level, use _tone position rules_ to apply new tone for
  the word. The override tone is always successful.

#### Scan pseudo-word

- Scan pseudo-word is a process to get the information needed from the existing characters to put
  the tone in the correct position.
- The existing characters must not be empty.
- Iterate backward from the last existing character (the new input is the tone trigger character).
- If a vowel is found first, continue go backward until scanned the first consonant (singular) or no
  character to scan, then stop.
- If a consonant is found first, continue go backward until found the first vowel, then continue go
  backward until scanned the first consonant (singular) or no character to scan, then stop.
- After iterated, a context have been formed either (in the left to right order, not the reverse)
  `<consonants>`, `<vowels><consonants>`, `<consonant><vowels><consonants>`, `<vowels>` or
  `<consonant><vowels>`.

#### Tone position rules

The process of applying tone to a word go through many steps:

- Focus on the `<vowels>` in peusdo-word, it could be one vowel but could be multiple vowels, the
  tone will be applied on one of these vowels.
- Exceptions:
  - Word exactly `QU` (and their lower cases), could not put tone, this is a consonant only.
- If one vowel, put the tone on that vowel.
- If multiple vowels, follow these rules, priority from top down:
  - Vowels has `Ơ` (and its lower case), put on the rightmost `Ơ`.
  - Vowels has one any of `Ê`, `Â`, `Ô`, `Ă`, `Ư` (and their lower cases), put on the rightmost
    listed vowel found by the reverse scan.
  - Word start with `GI`, `QU` (and their lower cases) and has more vowels, put on next vowel, `I` /
    `U` count as part of the consonant.
  - Vowels exactly `OA`, `OE`, `OO`, `UY` (and their lower cases), put on first vowel.
  - Vowels start with `OA`, `OE`, `OO`, `UY` (and their lower cases) and has more vowels or
    consonants, put on second vowel.
  - Otherwise, put on first vowel.
- Preserve case and diacritic on existing vowels.
- Could not put tone for other cases.

## Built-in fuzz testing API in Zig master / 0.16-era `std.testing`

### Public API surface

The public entry point is:

- [`std.testing.fuzz`](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/std/testing.zig#L32-L32) — re-exported through `std.testing` from the test runner.
- [`std.testing.FuzzInputOptions`](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/std/testing.zig#L1-L32) — options type accepted by `std.testing.fuzz`.

The actual implementation lives in the default test runner as [`pub fn fuzz`](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/compiler/test_runner.zig#L371-L375), with this high-level shape:

- first argument: `context: anytype`
- second argument: `testOne`, a comptime callback
- third argument: `options: testing.FuzzInputOptions`
- return type: `anyerror!void`

### Callback signature

The fuzz callback signature is:

- function name is user-defined, but commonly `testOne`
- accepts:
  - `context: @TypeOf(context)`
  - `input: []const u8`
- returns:
  - `anyerror!void`

Source: [`lib/compiler/test_runner.zig`](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/compiler/test_runner.zig#L371-L375).

So, conceptually:

- `context` is passed through from the `std.testing.fuzz` call.
- `input` is the fuzz-generated byte slice.
- any returned error other than `error.SkipZigTest` is treated as a fuzz/test failure; the runner prints diagnostics and exits nonzero ([`test_runner.zig` lines 400-418](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/compiler/test_runner.zig#L400-L418)).

### `FuzzInputOptions` fields

`FuzzInputOptions` currently has one high-level field:

- `corpus: []const []const u8 = &.{}` — initial corpus inputs supplied by the test author.

Source: [`lib/std/testing.zig`](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/std/testing.zig#L1-L32), found by repository search showing:

- `pub const FuzzInputOptions = struct { corpus: []const []const u8 = &.{}, };`

### Runtime behavior

The test runner distinguishes normal test execution from fuzz mode:

- In fuzz mode (`builtin.fuzz`), it:
  - initializes the fuzzer with the selected test’s callback,
  - feeds every `options.corpus` element into the fuzzer,
  - runs the fuzzer main loop with the selected limit/mode ([`test_runner.zig` lines 421-433](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/compiler/test_runner.zig#L421-L433)).

- Outside fuzz mode, it:
  - runs each provided corpus input once,
  - then always runs an empty-string smoke test ([`test_runner.zig` lines 436-444](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/compiler/test_runner.zig#L436-L444)).

### Build-system CLI invocation

Fuzzing is exposed through `zig build`, not as a separate `std.testing` function.

Relevant CLI flags:

- `zig build test --fuzz`
  - Enables the fuzzer for Zig test binaries in the build graph.
  - The default project template explicitly suggests passing `--fuzz` to `zig build test` for the fuzz example ([`lib/init/src/main.zig` lines 18-27](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/init/src/main.zig#L18-L27)).

- `--fuzz[=limit]`
  - Build runner help describes this as: continuously search for unit test failures with an optional maximum iteration limit ([`lib/compiler/build_runner.zig` lines 267-270](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/compiler/build_runner.zig#L267-L270), plus search result around the help text).
  - The parser accepts both `--fuzz` and `--fuzz=<limit>` ([`lib/compiler/build_runner.zig` search result for `--fuzz`](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/compiler/build_runner.zig)).

- `--seed <integer>`
  - Build runner flag used for shuffling dependency traversal order, defaulting to random; parsed as a `u32` ([`lib/compiler/build_runner.zig` lines 267-270](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/compiler/build_runner.zig#L267-L270)).
  - This affects build graph traversal/randomization, not the callback API itself.

The build web UI also documents `--fuzz` as enabling the fuzzer for Zig test binaries in the build graph, marked experimental ([`lib/build-web/index.html`](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/master/lib/build-web/index.html)).

## `FuzzInputOptions` fields

At `0.16.0`, [`FuzzInputOptions`](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/0.16.0/lib/std/testing.zig#L1210-L1212) has exactly one field:

- `corpus: []const []const u8 = &.{}`

No seed, max length, dictionary, or Smith-related fields exist in this struct.

## Normal test mode corpus execution

When the test executable is **not** built in fuzz mode, `std.testing.fuzz` only runs the provided corpus directly.

In [`lib/compiler/test_runner.zig`](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/blob/0.16.0/lib/compiler/test_runner.zig#L436-L444):

- it iterates `options.corpus`
- for each corpus entry, it calls `testOne(context, input)`
- after that, it always calls `testOne(context, "")` as an empty-input smoke test

So in normal test mode:

- every provided corpus entry is executed once
- the empty string is also executed once
- this empty-input call happens even if the corpus was non-empty

When built/run in fuzz mode, the test runner goes through the fuzzer ABI.

input.task: Critique this planned fuzz-testing approach for a Zig Vietnamese Telex input engine. Do not include any example code, pseudocode, or code-shaped snippets in your answer; give conceptual guidance only.
input.context:
Local repo: src/lex.zig is a single production file implementing a stateful Vietnamese Telex engine. Public ABI: lex_init, lex_add(state, ASCII alphabetic u8), lex_backspace(state), lex_calculate_synthetic_backspaces, lex_buffer_effective_full, lex_buffer_full, lex_buffer_empty, lex_compose_utf16_string_replacement. State has buffer_effective length 16, buffer_length u8, literal_index, buffer_modification_index. Existing unit tests in src/lex.zig cover Span mapping, diacritic apply/override/cancel, tone apply/override/cancel/reset, pseudoword scan, synthetic backspaces, replacement composition, raw allocation ABI. build.zig currently has a host addTest step for src/lex.zig and `zig build test`; production library is ReleaseSafe. Spec: inputs are ASCII alphabetic characters only; literal mode starts for F/J/W/Z at word start or F/J/W after invalid contexts; diacritics and tones mutate earlier spans; backspace can exit literal mode; callers use synthetic backspaces + UTF-16 replacement buffer after each add.

Initial approach to critique:
1. Use Zig's built-in std.testing.fuzz inside tests compiled from src/lex.zig, with a named fuzz test whose normal mode runs a fixed corpus and whose `zig build test --fuzz` mode lets Zig mutate inputs.
2. For Zig 0.16.0 specifically, verify the exact std.testing.fuzz callback signature before implementing. Evidence from the tag suggests FuzzInputOptions has a `corpus` field and callbacks receive `[]const u8`; some 0.16 release text mentions Smith, so this should be resolved against the actual compiler we pin.
3. Interpret fuzz bytes as a stream of operations, not merely text: add an ASCII letter, backspace if not empty, query booleans, calculate synthetic backspaces, compose replacement only when valid after an add and non-empty/effective buffer not beyond replacement constraints. Map arbitrary bytes into valid public API operations so fuzzing finds internal state bugs rather than assertion failures from documented precondition violations.
4. Prefer testing through exported/public ABI wrappers with raw allocated state at least for the main fuzz harness, because the Swift/macOS caller uses the C ABI. Optionally add a smaller internal State-level harness only if it reveals invariants not visible through ABI.
5. Core oracles/invariants: no crash/panic/assert for valid operation streams; buffer_empty/full/effective_full calls are consistent across operation sequence; synthetic backspace count never exceeds previous visible length and is zero when no retroactive edit occurred; replacement_count is within lex_replacement_buffer_length; each replacement UTF-16 code unit is ASCII or a valid Vietnamese code point produced by Span.to_utf16; after backspacing to empty, a fresh equivalent suffix behaves like a fresh state for add/composition; composing after add does not write beyond replacement_count.
6. Use a curated corpus emphasizing spec boundaries: empty/start F/J/W/Z, exact buffer length 15/16/17, uơ/ưo autofill with C/I/M/N/P/T/U and QU exclusions, diacritic apply/override/cancel, tone apply/override/cancel/reset, pseudo-word exceptions GI/QU and OA/OE/OO/UY, long literal tails, backspaces around literal_index.
7. Build integration: add a separate fuzz build step only if useful; otherwise `zig build test --fuzz` should target the existing test artifact. Keep ordinary `zig build test` deterministic and fast by relying on corpus-only execution in non-fuzz mode.
8. Because the local environment has Zig 0.15.2, do not implement until using/confirming Zig 0.16.0; the plan should mention version-gated API differences and avoid committing unverified code against 0.15.2.

run.result:
Recommendation: keep the fuzzing plan, but revise it around Zig 0.16’s Smith-based fuzz API and tighten the public-ABI operation model so the harness never calls functions outside their real caller contract. Scope: M, roughly 1–3h after a Zig 0.16.0 toolchain is available; more if you add a semantic reference model.

Key critiques and adjustments:

1. **Do not implement against the raw-byte callback assumption.**  
   The plan’s biggest risk is the `std.testing.fuzz` API assumption. Zig 0.16 release notes say the fuzz-test input changed from raw byte slices to `std.testing.Smith`. That means the main harness should generate structured operations with Smith, not depend on a callback receiving `[]const u8`. The project also has a toolchain mismatch: `.tool-versions` says Zig 0.15.2, while `build.zig.zon` requires 0.16.0. Resolve that before writing the test.

2. **Model the Swift caller contract exactly.**  
   The public functions have assertion-backed preconditions. The fuzzer should not call them in arbitrary order. In particular:
   - `lex_add` only with ASCII alphabetic input and only when not `lex_buffer_full`.
   - `lex_backspace` only when not `lex_buffer_empty`, matching the Swift wrapper.
   - `lex_calculate_synthetic_backspaces` only immediately after an `add` processed through the synthetic-replacement path.
   - `lex_compose_utf16_string_replacement` only when the effective buffer path is valid. The Swift caller checks `buffer_effective_full` before adding; if it is already full, it passes the original event through and does not compose replacement. Mirror that behavior. This matters because composition asserts that `buffer_length` is within the 16-span effective buffer.
   - Plain boolean queries are safe anytime after `lex_init`.

   This follows the actual macOS caller flow in [Lex.swift](macos/Lex.swift#L520-L597), not just the ABI names.

3. **Add `lex_init`/reset as a fuzz operation.**  
   The Swift layer resets the engine on spaces, modifiers, non-alphabetic input, and buffer-full recovery. The ABI does not expose a separate reset function, but callers use `lex_init` for reset. Fuzzing should include reset/reinit operations because they are part of real engine lifetime behavior.

4. **Strengthen the observable oracle.**  
   The proposed invariants are good but too weak if they only check “no panic” and bounds. Maintain an external visible-text model at the ABI level:
   - For a synthetic-path add, apply the returned synthetic backspace count to the model, then append the UTF-16 replacement.
   - For an effective-full/pass-through add, append the original ASCII input directly to the model and do not call compose.
   - For a real backspace, remove one visible UTF-16 unit from the model and call `lex_backspace`.
   - Assert no underflow, replacement count within the exported replacement capacity, and untouched replacement-buffer slots remain unchanged.

   This tests the ABI behavior the app actually relies on, instead of just internal consistency.

5. **Be careful with “replacement character is valid” checks.**  
   Do not validate replacement code units by calling the same production conversion path as the engine. That would mostly test the code against itself. Use an independently defined allowed set: ASCII alphabetic code units plus the Vietnamese BMP letters the spec allows. This is enough because the engine only emits single UTF-16 code units, not surrogate pairs.

6. **Use ABI fuzzing as the main harness; keep internal fuzzing optional.**  
   The main harness should use raw allocated state and exported functions, because that is the surface used by Swift and covered by [the ABI wrappers](src/lex.zig#L4028-L4198). An internal `State` harness is useful only for invariants not visible through the ABI, such as `literal_index`, `buffer_modification_index`, and exact span contents. Do not add it until the ABI harness is in place.

7. **Include buffer-length 255 behavior, not only 15/16/17.**  
   The corpus boundaries around the 16-span effective buffer are necessary, but the public ABI also exposes `lex_buffer_full`, and `State.append_literal` asserts before overflowing the `u8` buffer length. Add fuzz/corpus coverage for long literal tails near 254/255 and reset-at-full behavior. Do not let the fuzzer discover the documented overflow assertion by calling `lex_add` past full.

8. **Keep the curated corpus, but encode operation-level scenarios.**  
   The listed corpus topics are well chosen: literal starts, diacritic/tone apply/override/cancel/reset, `GI`/`QU`, `OA`/`OE`/`OO`/`UY`, autofill, backspaces around `literal_index`, and effective-buffer boundaries. With Smith, prefer weighting and operation generation for exploration, plus a deterministic corpus/replay path for targeted regressions and crash files. Keep seed cases short and focused; large sequences slow down mutation quality.

9. **Do not rely on unverified “corpus-only” normal test behavior.**  
   Zig 0.16 fuzzing behavior differs from older/raw-input designs. Verify whether normal `zig build test` runs only corpus seeds, a smoke fuzz pass, or some other bounded mode. Regardless, the fuzz test must be bounded and deterministic enough that ordinary `zig build test` remains fast.

10. **Build integration can stay simple.**  
   `build.zig` already creates a host test artifact for `src/lex.zig` in Debug mode and wires it to the `test` step in [build.zig](build.zig#L23-L35). A separate fuzz build step is unnecessary unless you need a different target, optimize mode, timeout, or named workflow. Keep production ReleaseSafe unchanged.

Bottom line: the plan is directionally sound, especially the decision to fuzz operation streams through the public ABI. The main corrections are to update it for Zig 0.16’s Smith API, emulate the Swift caller’s precondition-gated flow exactly, and add an external visible-text model so the fuzzer verifies real replacement behavior rather than only absence of crashes.

# Lex - Vietnamese Telex input method

The specification of the Lex program, a Vietnamese Telex input method.

## Vietnamese Telex Rules

### Literal input characters

- When any of the following characters start the word (when the word is empty), change to literal
  input from the new character position: `F`, `J`, `W`, `Z` (ignore cases), because these characters
  don't start a Vietnamese word. This rule is higher priority than diacritics and tones rules.
- When any of the following characters are added to the word, change to literal input from the new
  character position: `F`, `J`, `W` (ignore cases), because these characters don't appear in formal
  Vietnamese spelling. `Z` exists in Vietnamese word such as _Dzũng_, _Hồ Dzếnh_... This rule is
  lower priority than diacritics and tones rules.
- Literal input remains until the new word.
- When the user backspaces pass before the literal point, we switch to Vietnamese input again.

### Diacritics

Diacritics let a character have many variant. We only focus on character diacritics in this section.
Tones have a separate section.

#### Empty

- Any literal alphabet character has empty diacritic by default.
- Only a specific number of characters have other diacritic and it must follow the rules for those
  characters.

#### Circumflex

- Valid for: `A` (Â), `E` (Ê), `O` (Ô) and their lower cases.

#### Breve

- Valid for: `A` (Ă) and its lower case.

#### Horn

- Valid for: `O` (Ơ), `U` (Ư) and their lower cases.

#### Stroke

- Valid for: `D` (Đ) and its lower case.

#### Apply rules

- Only apply diacritic when the immediate previous character doesn't have any diacritic (empty).
- _Circumflex_, _stroke_ are triggered when user inputs the same character (ignore case) with the
  existing character when that character is valid for the applying diacritic.
  - `Aa` -> `Â`, `Ee` -> `Ê`, `Oo` -> `Ô`.
  - `Dd` -> `Đ`.
- _Breve_, _horn_ are triggered when user input `W`, `w` after the character when that character is
  valid for the applying diacritic. Otherwise, treat `W`, `w` literally.
  - `Aw` -> `Ă`.
  - `Ow` -> `Ơ`, `Uw` -> `Ư`.
- The existing character keep its case, tone.
- Treat out of scope characters as literal.

#### Override rules

- New valid diacritic can override existing valid diacritic of the same base character.
  - `Ăa` -> `Â`, `Âw` -> `Ă`.
  - `Ôw` -> `Ơ`, `Ơo` -> `Ô`.
- Only `A`, `O` have override rules because they have more than one possible character diacritic.
- Keep tone untouched.
- The existing character keep its case, tone.
- Treat out of scope characters as literal.

#### Cancel rules

- The cancellation is triggered if and only if user inputs the character (ignore case) that would
  produce the existing diacritic for the same base character of the immediate previous character.
- The existing character keeps its case, tone, but the diacritic is removed.
  - Circumflex: `Âa` -> `Aa`, `Ốo` -> `Óo`... and so on for other cases of the same kind.
  - Breve: `Ăw` -> `Aw`.
  - Horn: `Ưw` -> `Uw`... and so on for other cases of the same kind.
  - Stroke: `Đd` -> `Dd`, `đD` -> `dD`.
- The new character is literal, keeps its case, no tone.
- Switch to literal from the new character position and the following characters. Literal input
  remains until the new word.
  - Existing `Â`, input `aa`, result `Aaa`.
- When the user backspaces pass before the literal point, we switch to Vietnamese input again.

#### Auto-fill rules

- The auto-fill is only applied for `ươ` syllable immediately before the user input, when one of the
  character in the syllable is missing horn: `uơ` and `ưo`.
- Fill the missing _horn_ when the input is one of these character (ignore case): `C`, `I`, `M`,
  `N`, `P`, `T`, `U` and their lower cases.
  - Fill missing horn on `U`: `uơn` -> `ươn`.
  - Fill missing horn on `O`: `ưóp` -> `ướp`.
- The new input character is appended literally.
- Tone and case of existing characters are preserved on the original characters.

### Tones

Tones let a word have many variants, each variant has different meaning. Only the following
Vietnamese vowel could have tones: `A`, `E`, `I`, `O`, `U`, `Y` and their corresponding variants.
These vowel could take any tone.

#### Level (ngang)

- The default tone, it's the vowel without any tone mark, e.g. `A`, `Ê`, `Ơ`...and all other
  corresponding variants.
- If a vowel has tone mark other than level, use `Z`, `z` to reset the tone to level.

#### Rising (sắc)

- Example of rising tone: `Á`, `Ế`, `Ớ`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `S`, `s` to put the rising tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `As` -> `Á`, `Ês` -> `Ế`, `Ơs`
  -> `Ớ`.

#### Falling (huyền)

- Example of falling tone: `À`, `Ề`, `Ờ`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `F`, `f` to put the falling tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `Af` -> `À`, `Êf` -> `Ề`, `Ơf`
  -> `Ờ`.

#### Dipping-rising (hỏi)

- Example of dipping-rising tone: `Ả`, `Ể`, `Ở`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `R`, `r` to put the dipping-rising tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `Ar` -> `Ả`, `Êr` ->
  `Ể`, `Ơr` -> `Ở`.

#### Rising-glottalized (ngã)

- Example of rising-glottalized tone: `Ã`, `Ễ`, `Ỡ`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `X`, `x` to put the rising-glottalized tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `Ax` -> `Ã`, `Êx`
  -> `Ễ`, `Ơx` -> `Ỡ`.

#### Falling-glottalized (nặng)

- Example of falling-glottalized tone: `Ạ`, `Ệ`, `Ợ`...and all other corresponding variants.
- Use `J`, `j` to put the falling-glottalized tone to the Vietnamese vowels, e.g. `Aj` -> `Ạ`, `Êj`
  -> `Ệ`, `Ơj` -> `Ợ`.

#### Apply rules

- Only trigger apply tone when the buffer has existing characters. Otherwise, append the new
  character literally.
- Trigger apply tone when user inputs the trigger character for tones: `S`, `F`, `R`, `X`, `J` and
  their lower cases.
- _Scan pseudo-word_ to have the information for later steps.
- If the pseudo-word doesn't have any vowels, append new character literally.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and all of them don't have any tone (level), use _tone
  position rules_ to apply the tone for the word.
- If _tone position rules_ could not put tone to the pseudo-word, append new character literally.

#### Cancel rules

- Only trigger apply tone when the buffer has existing characters. Otherwise, append the new
  character literally.
- Trigger apply tone when user inputs the trigger character for tones: `S`, `F`, `R`, `X`, `J` and
  their lower cases.
- _Scan pseudo-word_ to have the information for later steps.
- If the pseudo-word doesn't have any vowels, handle by _apply rules_.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and has the tone (other than level) on vowels match with
  the triggered tone. Reset that tone to level. Append new character literally.
- If the new character has been appended literally, switch to literal from the new character
  position and the following characters. Literal input remains until the new word.
- When the user backspaces pass before the literal point, we switch to Vietnamese input again.

#### Reset rules

- Only trigger reset tone when the buffer has existing characters. Otherwise, append the new
  character literally.
- Trigger reset tone when user inputs the trigger character for reset: `Z`, `z`.
- _Scan pseudo-word_ to have the information for later steps.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and has tone (other than level) in one of the vowels,
  change that tone to level, keep case and diacritic.
- If the pseudo-word doesn't have any vowels, append the new character literally and remain
  Vietnamese input to continue process Vietnamese input such as `dzu + x` -> `dzũ`.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and all of them don't have any tone (level), append the
  new character literally and switch to literal from the new character position and the following
  characters. Literal input remains until the new word.
- When the user backspaces pass before the literal point, we switch to Vietnamese input again.

#### Override rules

- Only trigger override tone when the buffer has existing characters. Otherwise, append the new
  character literally.
- Trigger apply tone when user inputs the trigger character for tones: `S`, `F`, `R`, `X`, `J` and
  their lower cases.
- _Scan pseudo-word_ to have the information for later steps.
- If the pseudo-word doesn't have any vowels, handle by _apply rules_.
- If the pseudo-word has at least one vowel and has the tone (other than level) on vowels different
  from the triggered tone, reset that tone to level, use _tone position rules_ to apply new tone for
  the word. The override tone is always successful.

#### Scan pseudo-word

- Scan pseudo-word is a process to get the information needed from the existing characters to put
  the tone in the correct position.
- The existing characters must not be empty.
- Iterate backward from the last existing character (the new input is the tone trigger character).
- If a vowel is found first, continue go backward until scanned the first consonant (singular) or no
  character to scan, then stop.
- If a consonant is found first, continue go backward until found the first vowel, then continue go
  backward until scanned the first consonant (singular) or no character to scan, then stop.
- After iterated, a context have been formed either (in the left to right order, not the reverse)
  `<consonants>`, `<vowels><consonants>`, `<consonant><vowels><consonants>`, `<vowels>` or
  `<consonant><vowels>`.

#### Tone position rules

The process of applying tone to a word go through many steps:

- Focus on the `<vowels>` in peusdo-word, it could be one vowel but could be multiple vowels, the
  tone will be applied on one of these vowels.
- Exceptions:
  - Word exactly `QU` (and their lower cases), could not put tone, this is a consonant only.
- If one vowel, put the tone on that vowel.
- If multiple vowels, follow these rules, priority from top down:
  - Vowels has `Ơ` (and its lower case), put on the rightmost `Ơ`.
  - Vowels has one any of `Ê`, `Â`, `Ô`, `Ă`, `Ư` (and their lower cases), put on the rightmost
    listed vowel found by the reverse scan.
  - Word start with `GI`, `QU` (and their lower cases) and has more vowels, put on next vowel, `I` /
    `U` count as part of the consonant.
  - Vowels exactly `OA`, `OE`, `OO`, `UY` (and their lower cases), put on first vowel.
  - Vowels start with `OA`, `OE`, `OO`, `UY` (and their lower cases) and has more vowels or
    consonants, put on second vowel.
  - Otherwise, put on first vowel.
- Preserve case and diacritic on existing vowels.
- Could not put tone for other cases.

# 8 Unit tests
## 8.1 Introducing the `test` block
```
 const  std =  @import ( "std" );  const  expect = std.testing.expect;  test "testing simple sum" {  const  a:  u8  =  2 ;  const  b:  u8  =  2 ;  try  expect((a + b) ==  4 );  }
```
```
1/1 file4eb435a7450e.test.testing simple sum...OKA
  All 1 tests passed.
```
You can have multiple `test` blocks written on the same Zig module. Also, you can mix `test` blocks with your source code, with no problems or consequences. If you mix `test` blocks with your normal source code, when you execute the `build` , `build-exe` , `build-obj` or `build-lib` commands from the `zig` compiler that we exposed in Section 1.2.5 , these `test` blocks are automatically ignored by the compiler.
In other words, the `zig` compiler builds and execute your unit tests only when you ask it to. By default, the compiler always ignore `test` blocks written in your Zig modules. The compiler normally checks only if there are any syntax errors in these `test` blocks.
If you take a look at the source code for most of the files present in the Zig Standard Library ¹ , you can see that the `test` blocks are written together with the normal source code of the library. You can see this for example, at the [`array_list` module](https://codeberg.org/ziglang/zig/src/branch/master/lib/std/array_list.zig) ² . So, the standard that the Zig developers decided to adopt is to keep their unit tests together with the source code of the functionality that they are testing.

...

## 8.3 Testing memory allocations
One of the advantages of Zig is that it offers great tools that help us, programmers, to avoid (but also detect) memory problems, such as memory leaks and double-frees. The `defer` keyword is especially helpful in this regard.
When developing your source code, you, the programmer, are responsible for making sure that your code does not produce such problems. However, you can also use a special type of an allocator object in Zig that is capable of automatically detecting such problems for you. This is the `std.testing.allocator` object. This allocator object offers some basic memory safety detection features, which are capable of detecting memory leaks.

...

## 8.4 Testing errors
But in Zig, we use the `expectError()` function, from the `std.testing` module. With this function, you can test if a specific function call returns the exact type of error that you expect it to return. To use this function, you first write `try expectError()` . Then, on the first argument, you provide the type of error that you are expecting from the function call. Then, on the second argument, you write the function call that you expect to fail.
The code example below demonstrates such type of unit test in Zig. Notice that, inside the function `alloc_error()` we are allocating 100 bytes of memory, or, an array of 100 elements, for the object `ibuffer` . However, in the `test` block, we are using the `FixedBufferAllocator()` allocator object, which is limited to 10 bytes of space, because the object `buffer` , which we provided to the allocator object, have only 10 bytes of space.
That is why, the `alloc_error()` function raises an `OutOfMemory` error on this case. Because this function is trying to allocate more space than the allocator object allows. So, in essence, we are testing for a specific type of error, which is `OutOfMemory` . If the `alloc_error()` function returns any other type of error, then, the `expectError()` function would make the entire test fail.
```
 const  std =  @import ( "std" );  const  Allocator = std.mem.Allocator;  const  expectError = std.testing.expectError;  fn  alloc_error(allocator: Allocator) ! void {  var  ibuffer =  try  allocator.alloc( u8 ,  100 );  defer  allocator.free(ibuffer);      ibuffer[ 0 ] =  2 ;  }   test "testing error" {  var  buffer: [ 10 ] u8  =  undefined ;  var  fba = std.heap.FixedBufferAllocator.init(&buffer);  const  allocator = fba.allocator();  try  expectError( error .OutOfMemory, alloc_error(allocator));  }
```

...

## 8.5 Testing simple equalities
```
 const  std =  @import ( "std" );  test "values are equal?" {  const  v1 =  15 ;  const  v2 =  18 ;  try  std.testing.expectEqual(v1, v2);  }
```
```
1/1 ve.test.values are equal?...
    expected 15, found 18
    FAIL (TestExpectedEqual)
ve.zig:5:5: test.values are equal? (test)
    try std.testing.expectEqual(v1, v2);
    ^
0 passed; 0 skipped; 1 failed.
```
Although useful, the `expectEqual()` function does not work with arrays. For testing if two arrays are equal, you should use the `expectEqualSlices()` function instead. This function have three arguments. First, you provide the data type contained in both arrays that you are trying to compare. While the second and third arguments corresponds to the array objects that you want to compare.
In the example below, we are using this function to test if two array objects ( `array1` and `array2` ) are equal or not. Since they are in fact equal, the unit test passed with no errors.
```
 const  std =  @import ( "std" );  test "arrays are equal?" {  const  array1 = [ 3 ] u32 { 1 ,  2 ,  3 } ;  const  array2 = [ 3 ] u32 { 1 ,  2 ,  3 } ;  try  std.testing.expectEqualSlices(  u32 , &array1, &array2      );  }
```
```
1/1 file4eb4677d87a.test.arrays are equal?...OKAll
  l 1 tests passed.
```
At last, you might also want to use the `expectEqualStrings()` function. As the name suggests, you can use this function to test if two strings are equal or not. Just provide the two string objects that you want to compare, as inputs to the function.
If the function finds any existing differences between the two strings, then, the function will raise an error, and also, print an error message that shows the exact difference between the two string objects provided, as the example below demonstrates:
```
 const  std =  @import ( "std" );  test "strings are equal?" {  const  str1 =  "hello, world!" ;  const  str2 =  "Hello, world!" ;  try  std.testing.expectEqualStrings(          str1, str2      );  }
```
```
1/1 t.test.strings are equal?...
====== expected this output: =========
hello, world!␃
======== instead found this: =========
Hello, world!␃
======================================
First difference occurs on line 1:
expected:
hello, world!
^ ('\x68')
found:
Hello, world!
^ ('\x48')
```

# Fuzzing Zig Code Using AFL++
2021-09-19 - Programming - Zig - Fuzzing
_Last updated 2022-05-08_ ( [changelog](https://github.com/squeek502/ryanliptak.com/commits/master/posts/fuzzing-zig-code.md) )
After [using code coverage information and real-world files](https://www.ryanliptak.com/blog/code-coverage-zig-callgrind/) to improve an [audio metadata parser](https://github.com/squeek502/audiometa) I am writing in [Zig](https://ziglang.org/) , the next step was to fuzz test it in order to ensure that crashes, memory leaks, etc were ironed out as much as possible.

...

## Treating zig code as a black box 🔗
```
const std = @import ( "std" ); const audiometa = @import ( "audiometa" ); pub fn main () ! void { // Setup an allocator that will detect leaks/use-after-free/etc var gpa = std . heap . GeneralPurposeAllocator (.{}){}; // this will check for leaks and crash the program if it finds any defer std . debug . assert ( gpa . deinit () == false ); const allocator = gpa . allocator (); // Read the data from stdin const stdin = std . io . getStdIn (); const data = try stdin . readToEndAlloc ( allocator , std . math . maxInt ( usize )); defer allocator . free ( data ); var stream_source = std . io . StreamSource { . buffer = std . io . fixedBufferStream ( data ) }; // Try to parse the data var metadata = try audiometa . metadata . readAll ( allocator , & stream_source ); defer metadata . deinit (); }
```
Note: `afl++` passes the fuzzed data in via `stdin` by default
With this, I tried a few of the black-box options that `afl++` has:

...

* I wasn't checking for possible text data size underflows
* I wasn't protecting against out-of-bounds reads when checking UTF-16 BOMs
* A few more data size underflow/index out-of-bounds protections were needed elsewhere
* I wasn't handling malformed extended ID3v2 headers safely
* [There was a bug in the Zig standard library where the `std.unicode` functions that allocated memory would fail to free the memory if they returned an error](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/pull/9776)
Despite the success, I felt that things could be improved.

...

## Treating zig code as a static library 🔗
```
const std = @import ( "std" ); const audiometa = @import ( "audiometa" ); // export the zig function so that it can be called from C export fn fuzz_zig_main () void { // code omitted--it's the same as the previous example, // but with the try's swapped out for catch unreachable's }
```
```
// fuzz_lib.h void fuzz_zig_main ();
```
```
// fuzz.c #include "fuzz_lib.h" int main () { fuzz_zig_main (); return 0 ; }
```
I was then able to compile the Zig portion as a static library:
* with LTO (passing `-flto` or setting `LibExeObjStep.want_lto = true` )
* with compiler_rt bundled [to avoid `undefined symbol: __zig_probe_stack` linker errors](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/issues/6817) (passing `-fcompiler-rt` or setting `LibExeObjStep.bundle_compiler_rt = true` )
and then compile the C portion via `afl-clang-lto` and link in the Zig portion:

...

## Skipping the C code 🔗
```
const std = @import ( "std" ); fn cMain () callconv (. C ) void { main () catch unreachable ; } comptime { @export ( cMain , .{ . name = "main" , . linkage = . Strong }); } pub fn main () ! void { var gpa = std . heap . GeneralPurposeAllocator (.{}){}; // this will check for leaks and crash the program if it finds any defer std . debug . assert ( gpa . deinit () == false ); const allocator = gpa . allocator (); const stdin = std . io . getStdIn (); const data = try stdin . readToEndAlloc ( allocator , std . math . maxInt ( usize )); defer allocator . free ( data ); if ( data . len == 0 ) return ; switch ( data [ 0 ]) { 0 => { // alloc without free _ = try allocator . alloc ( u8 , 10 ); }, 1 => { // returning an error return error . BadInput ; }, else => {}, } }
```

...

However, neither the CLI interface nor the build system interface is needed in order to enable fuzzing. The only thing that is needed is to ask for fuzz input in unit tests, as in the above example.
When the build runner interacts with the test runner, it learns which tests, if any, are fuzz tests. Then when unit tests pass, it moves on to fuzz testing, by providing our own implementation of the genetic algorithms that drive the input bytes (similar to [libFuzzer](https://llvm.org/docs/LibFuzzer.html) or [AFL](https://lcamtuf.coredump.cx/afl/) ), and re-compiling the unit test binary with `-ffuzz` enabled.
Fuzz testing is level-driven so we will need some CLI to operate those options. For example, `zig build --fuzz` might start fuzzing indefinitely, while `zig build --fuzz=300s` declares success after fuzzing for five minutes. When fuzz testing is not requested, it defaults to a small number of iterations just to smoke test that it's all working.
Some sort of UI would be nice. For starters this could just be `std.Progress` . In the future perhaps there could be a live-updating HTML page to visualize progress and code coverage in realtime. The fuzzer now is able to utilize multiple cores. This is controllable
with the `-j` build option. Limited fuzzing still uses one core.

### Fuzzing Infinite Mode §

When provided multiple tests, the fuzzer now switches between them and prioritizes the most
effective and interesting ones. Over time already explored tests will become barely run compared
to tests yielding new inputs.

### Crash Dumps §

Crashing inputs are now saved to a file indicated by the crash message. It is recommended to
use these files to reproduce the crash using `std.testing.FuzzInputOptions.corpus` and `@embedFile` .

### Numerous bugs found and fixed with the help of an AST smith §

The new smith interface has already seen use in testing the toolchain with the creation of an
AST Smith which is used to generate random valid ASTs.

When run against zig fmt (in addition to some earlier simpler random
source testing) 20 unique bugs were found and fixed, some of which had
been previously reported and many newly discovered.

It also found several inconsistencies between the specified PEG and the parser:
notably, a tuple could not contain types starting with `extern` or `inline` ; for example, `const T = struct { u64 , extern struct { a: u64 }, u32 }` would result in an error. A detailed list of PEG and Parser changes can be found on [add an ast smith](https://codeberg.org/ziglang/zig/pulls/31635) .

## Bug Fixes §

Full list of the 345 bug reports closed during this release cycle:

* [Tracked on GitHub](https://github.com/ziglang/zig/issues?q=is%3Aclosed+is%3Aissue+label%3Abug+milestone%3A0.16.0)

Recommendation: keep the fuzzing plan, but revise it around Zig 0.16’s Smith-based fuzz API and tighten the public-ABI operation model so the harness never calls functions outside their real caller contract. Scope: M, roughly 1–3h after a Zig 0.16.0 toolchain is available; more if you add a semantic reference model.

Key critiques and adjustments:

1. **Do not implement against the raw-byte callback assumption.**  
   The plan’s biggest risk is the `std.testing.fuzz` API assumption. Zig 0.16 release notes say the fuzz-test input changed from raw byte slices to `std.testing.Smith`. That means the main harness should generate structured operations with Smith, not depend on a callback receiving `[]const u8`. The project also has a toolchain mismatch: `.tool-versions` says Zig 0.15.2, while `build.zig.zon` requires 0.16.0. Resolve that before writing the test.

2. **Model the Swift caller contract exactly.**  
   The public functions have assertion-backed preconditions. The fuzzer should not call them in arbitrary order. In particular:
   - `lex_add` only with ASCII alphabetic input and only when not `lex_buffer_full`.
   - `lex_backspace` only when not `lex_buffer_empty`, matching the Swift wrapper.
   - `lex_calculate_synthetic_backspaces` only immediately after an `add` processed through the synthetic-replacement path.
   - `lex_compose_utf16_string_replacement` only when the effective buffer path is valid. The Swift caller checks `buffer_effective_full` before adding; if it is already full, it passes the original event through and does not compose replacement. Mirror that behavior. This matters because composition asserts that `buffer_length` is within the 16-span effective buffer.
   - Plain boolean queries are safe anytime after `lex_init`.

   This follows the actual macOS caller flow in [Lex.swift](macos/Lex.swift#L520-L597), not just the ABI names.

3. **Add `lex_init`/reset as a fuzz operation.**  
   The Swift layer resets the engine on spaces, modifiers, non-alphabetic input, and buffer-full recovery. The ABI does not expose a separate reset function, but callers use `lex_init` for reset. Fuzzing should include reset/reinit operations because they are part of real engine lifetime behavior.

4. **Strengthen the observable oracle.**  
   The proposed invariants are good but too weak if they only check “no panic” and bounds. Maintain an external visible-text model at the ABI level:
   - For a synthetic-path add, apply the returned synthetic backspace count to the model, then append the UTF-16 replacement.
   - For an effective-full/pass-through add, append the original ASCII input directly to the model and do not call compose.
   - For a real backspace, remove one visible UTF-16 unit from the model and call `lex_backspace`.
   - Assert no underflow, replacement count within the exported replacement capacity, and untouched replacement-buffer slots remain unchanged.

   This tests the ABI behavior the app actually relies on, instead of just internal consistency.

5. **Be careful with “replacement character is valid” checks.**  
   Do not validate replacement code units by calling the same production conversion path as the engine. That would mostly test the code against itself. Use an independently defined allowed set: ASCII alphabetic code units plus the Vietnamese BMP letters the spec allows. This is enough because the engine only emits single UTF-16 code units, not surrogate pairs.

6. **Use ABI fuzzing as the main harness; keep internal fuzzing optional.**  
   The main harness should use raw allocated state and exported functions, because that is the surface used by Swift and covered by [the ABI wrappers](src/lex.zig#L4028-L4198). An internal `State` harness is useful only for invariants not visible through the ABI, such as `literal_index`, `buffer_modification_index`, and exact span contents. Do not add it until the ABI harness is in place.

7. **Include buffer-length 255 behavior, not only 15/16/17.**  
   The corpus boundaries around the 16-span effective buffer are necessary, but the public ABI also exposes `lex_buffer_full`, and `State.append_literal` asserts before overflowing the `u8` buffer length. Add fuzz/corpus coverage for long literal tails near 254/255 and reset-at-full behavior. Do not let the fuzzer discover the documented overflow assertion by calling `lex_add` past full.

8. **Keep the curated corpus, but encode operation-level scenarios.**  
   The listed corpus topics are well chosen: literal starts, diacritic/tone apply/override/cancel/reset, `GI`/`QU`, `OA`/`OE`/`OO`/`UY`, autofill, backspaces around `literal_index`, and effective-buffer boundaries. With Smith, prefer weighting and operation generation for exploration, plus a deterministic corpus/replay path for targeted regressions and crash files. Keep seed cases short and focused; large sequences slow down mutation quality.

9. **Do not rely on unverified “corpus-only” normal test behavior.**  
   Zig 0.16 fuzzing behavior differs from older/raw-input designs. Verify whether normal `zig build test` runs only corpus seeds, a smoke fuzz pass, or some other bounded mode. Regardless, the fuzz test must be bounded and deterministic enough that ordinary `zig build test` remains fast.

10. **Build integration can stay simple.**  
   `build.zig` already creates a host test artifact for `src/lex.zig` in Debug mode and wires it to the `test` step in [build.zig](build.zig#L23-L35). A separate fuzz build step is unnecessary unless you need a different target, optimize mode, timeout, or named workflow. Keep production ReleaseSafe unchanged.

Bottom line: the plan is directionally sound, especially the decision to fuzz operation streams through the public ABI. The main corrections are to update it for Zig 0.16’s Smith API, emulate the Swift caller’s precondition-gated flow exactly, and add an external visible-text model so the fuzzer verifies real replacement behavior rather than only absence of crashes.

- in fuzz mode, corpus entries are submitted to the fuzzer;

input.context:
Repo context: Vietnamese Telex engine in src/lex.zig. Production code must not be changed. Current fuzz harness is test-only at end of src/lex.zig. It uses std.testing.fuzz with *std.testing.Smith, public ABI only, raw allocated state, operation stream with add/backspace/reset/query/add_again. It maps adds to ASCII alphabetic characters, mirrors caller preconditions, resets before buffer_full, avoids replacement composition when buffer_effective_full was already true, maintains an external visible UTF-16 buffer and word_start, applies synthetic backspaces then appends replacement, checks replacement_count bounds, untouched sentinel slots, allowed UTF-16 code points, and simple buffer query invariants. Zig 0.16.0 test build has .error_tracing=false due fuzz runner compile issue. Verification passed `zig build test`, `zig build test --fuzz=1`, `--fuzz=100`.

Goal: elaborate from here to make fuzzing more comprehensive and still solid. Potential directions under consideration:
1. Improve operation generation: use Smith enums/weighted operations instead of byte modulo; add weighted letters favoring Telex triggers and Vietnamese edge cases; add longer sequences to hit 255 buffer_full while keeping model bounded.
2. Add more stateful assertions based on app contract: fresh-state equivalence after reset; after backspacing to word_start, next add should match fresh state output; query invariants across exact buffer lengths.
3. Add semantic metamorphic properties that avoid duplicating production logic: case preservation for paired inputs, reset equivalence, pass-through/literal tail behavior, no-op query non-mutating behavior.
4. Add independent output validator: a table of exact allowed Vietnamese codepoints rather than broad 0x1EA0...0x1EF9 range; maybe validate at most one non-level tone in the current visible word if independently tractable.
5. Split fuzz targets: one public ABI app-flow fuzz target, one public ABI long-literal/full-buffer fuzz target, maybe one internal State invariant target only if its value outweighs coupling to implementation.
6. Add corpus management: encode named scenario seeds for all spec rules; include crash reproducer files via FuzzInputOptions.corpus when found; document commands for limited and infinite fuzz runs.
7. Add negative/precondition fuzzing? Probably not in std.testing.fuzz because asserts are documented, but maybe separate unit tests for wrapper guards.

Please critique priorities, risks of overfitting/false positives, and recommend a staged plan. No code examples.

Primary recommendation: keep the current public-ABI app-flow harness as the canonical fuzz target, then add one focused public-ABI full-buffer target and strengthen the independent oracle. Defer internal `State` fuzzing and negative/precondition fuzzing unless a concrete bug class appears that the public harness cannot expose.

Priority order:

1. **Dedicated full-buffer / long-literal ABI target**
2. **Exact independent output validator**
3. **Cheap public-contract state assertions**
4. **Better weighted operation and character generation**
5. **Selective metamorphic properties**
6. **Corpus/reproducer hygiene**
7. **Internal and negative fuzzing only if justified later**

## Critique of the proposed directions

### 1. Operation generation: useful, but not the first correctness upgrade

Improving generation is worthwhile, but the current biggest gap is not modulo bias; it is that the harness does not reliably reach the `255` buffer-full boundary.

Use weighted generation, but preserve broad exploration:

- Adds should dominate, otherwise the fuzzer will spend too much time resetting, querying, or backspacing shallow states.
- Queries should be low weight because they do not advance state.
- Backspaces and resets need enough weight to exercise state clearing, cancellation, and replay paths, but not so much that long composition runs become rare.
- Telex trigger letters, vowels, uppercase variants, and special placement families should be favored.
- Keep a nonzero path for ordinary ASCII letters so the fuzzer still explores literal tails and uninteresting-looking consonant runs.

Risk: if the generator becomes too grammar-like, it may only test known Vietnamese/Telex scenarios and miss weird but valid ASCII operation streams. The harness should remain an operation-stream fuzzer, not a miniature Telex parser.

For longer sequences, do not simply raise the app-flow operation cap. Long inputs have different performance and modeling needs. Put the `254/255` behavior in a separate target so the normal app-flow target remains fast and mutation-friendly.

Effort: **M, 1–3h**.

---

### 2. Stateful assertions: high value if scoped to observable public behavior

These are good next additions, especially because they avoid duplicating production composition logic.

Prioritize:

- **Immediate reset invariants:** after reset, public query state should match a fresh state.
- **Fresh-state equivalence after reset:** behavior after reset should match behavior from a newly initialized state for the same subsequent operations.
- **Backspace-to-word-start equivalence:** only assert this when the public state is actually empty and the external visible model says the current word is empty. Do not infer freshness from visible length alone.
- **Query idempotence:** repeated buffer queries should return stable results and should not affect later observable behavior.

The strongest version of “query is non-mutating” requires comparing two public states: one with queries inserted, one without. Repeated query flags alone can miss a query that mutates hidden state but leaves booleans temporarily unchanged.

For exact buffer lengths, only assert exact expectations in controlled literal runs where the harness independently knows the engine should be at length `0`, `1`, `15`, `16`, `254`, or `255`. Avoid asserting exact length-derived behavior in arbitrary Telex sequences unless the model truly owns that state.

Effort: **M, 1–3h** for basic assertions; **M–L, 3h–1d** for two-state equivalence checks.

---

### 3. Metamorphic properties: good, but choose conservative ones first

Best first properties:

- **Reset equivalence:** prefix, reset, suffix behaves like fresh state on the suffix.
- **Query insertion equivalence:** adding queries between mutating operations does not change later observable output.
- **Pass-through after effective-full:** when the app contract says composition is skipped, the visible output should append the raw ASCII input and preserve the existing visible prefix.
- **Backspace-to-empty equivalence:** once the current word has been erased and public state reports empty, the next add should behave like a fresh first add.

Be cautious with:

- **Case preservation.** This is valuable for finding upper/lower mapping bugs, but only after the exact expected relation is specified. General “uppercase input equals uppercase output” can be false for mixed-case edge cases, titlecase-like behavior, or trigger handling. Start with narrow paired scenarios whose behavior is explicitly part of the spec.
- **Literal-tail behavior outside effective-full.** Literal pass-through is safe to assert only where the app contract clearly says composition is bypassed.

Avoid metamorphic properties that silently become a second implementation of Telex rules. The best properties compare observable behavior under equivalent public histories, not expected linguistic output.

Effort: **M–L, 3h–1d**.

---

### 4. Independent output validator: exact table is high priority

Tightening the allowed UTF-16 validator is one of the best upgrades.

The current broad ranges can admit wrong-but-nearby Latin code points. An exact table of allowed output characters is more independent and more useful than many additional random operations. It should include:

- ASCII alphabetic characters the public ABI accepts.
- Exact uppercase and lowercase Vietnamese precomposed characters the engine is specified to emit.
- No broad Latin ranges unless every code point in the range is intentionally allowed.

This catches table-indexing mistakes, wrong case mappings, wrong diacritic variants, and accidental emission of unrelated Latin Extended characters.

The “at most one non-level tone” property is plausible but should come later. It needs an independent tone classifier and careful scoping to the current active word. It should not be applied to arbitrary visible text across resets or simulated word boundaries unless the model’s `word_start` contract is exact.

Effort: **M, 1–3h** for exact allowed set; **M–L** for tone-category validation.

---

### 5. Split fuzz targets: yes, do this

Do not make one monolithic fuzz target responsible for app flow, long buffer boundaries, metamorphic replay, and internal invariants. The goals conflict.

Recommended targets:

#### A. Public ABI app-flow target

Keep this as the main harness.

Purpose:

- Realistic caller operation streams.
- Add, backspace, reset, query, add-again.
- External visible buffer model.
- Synthetic backspace and replacement checks.
- General invariant checking.

Keep operation count moderate so normal tests and short fuzz runs stay useful.

Effort to maintain: **S**.

#### B. Public ABI long-literal / full-buffer target

Add a focused target for:

- Effective-full transition around the small composition boundary.
- Long literal tails after effective-full.
- Exact `254/255` full-buffer behavior.
- Reset-before-add once full.
- Query invariants at known controlled lengths.

This target should use controlled mostly-literal input so the harness can independently know what boundary it is exercising. It should still use the public ABI and the same app preconditions.

This is the most concrete current coverage gap.

Effort: **M, 1–3h**.

#### C. Optional public ABI metamorphic target

If the app-flow target becomes too complex, put two-state equivalence checks here instead of complicating the main harness.

Purpose:

- Reset equivalence.
- Query insertion equivalence.
- Backspace-to-empty equivalence.
- Narrow case-pair relations.

Effort: **M–L, 3h–1d**.

#### D. Internal `State` target

Defer.

Only add this if:

- Public ABI fuzzing finds bugs that are hard to minimize/localize.
- There are important internal invariants not observable through the ABI.
- Refactoring internal state becomes risky enough to justify coupling tests to implementation.

If added, keep it about structural invariants, not expected Telex output. Otherwise it will become brittle and duplicate production logic.

Effort: **L, 1–2d**, and higher maintenance cost.

---

### 6. Corpus management: necessary, but keep it lean

Good corpus policy:

- Keep seeds short and named/commented by scenario.
- Add one or two long boundary seeds only to the full-buffer target, not the general app-flow target.
- Include minimized crash reproducers once found.
- Avoid adding many similar long seeds; they slow normal test replay and reduce mutation quality.
- Document limited fuzz runs, longer local runs, and infinite/manual fuzzing separately.

For Zig 0.16, be careful with “files” as corpus. If `FuzzInputOptions` only accepts in-source byte slices, store minimized reproducers there with clear labels. Do not build a custom file-loading corpus path unless there is a strong reason; it adds moving parts and may make normal tests less hermetic.

Effort: **S–M, <1–3h**.

---

### 7. Negative/precondition fuzzing: mostly do not do it

Do not put invalid ABI calls into `std.testing.fuzz` if the public contract documents those calls as precondition violations. The fuzzer will mostly rediscover expected assertions.

Useful negative coverage belongs elsewhere:

- Unit tests for wrapper-level guards, if such guards are supposed to recover or reject cleanly.
- Tests for the higher-level caller that proves it does not call the ABI while full, empty, or with invalid input.
- No fuzzing of documented assertion failures unless the goal is specifically to test trap behavior.

Effort: **S** if there are wrapper guards; otherwise skip.

## Recommended staged plan

### Stage 1 — Strengthen the oracle without broadening behavior

Effort: **M, 1–3h**

Do first:

1. Replace broad allowed Unicode ranges with an exact independent allowed-output set.
2. Add immediate reset/fresh query invariants.
3. Add repeated-query stability checks.
4. Add stronger sentinel and visible-prefix checks where the current app contract already determines the result.
5. Keep all assertions public-ABI based.

This improves bug detection before increasing the input space.

Success criteria:

- Normal test run remains fast.
- Existing fuzz runs still pass.
- Validator cannot accept unrelated Latin code points just because they fall in a broad range.

---

### Stage 2 — Add the dedicated full-buffer target

Effort: **M, 1–3h**

Add a separate public-ABI target focused on:

1. Effective-full boundary.
2. Literal tail after effective-full.
3. Exact near-full and full states.
4. Reset-before-add behavior once full.
5. Query behavior at controlled known lengths.

Keep it controlled and bounded. Do not let this target call `lex_add` past full. That would test a caller bug, not an engine bug.

Success criteria:

- Corpus replay deterministically reaches the `255` full-buffer state.
- The target verifies behavior immediately before full, at full, and after reset.
- App-flow fuzz target remains moderate-sized and fast.

---

### Stage 3 — Improve generation and corpus

Effort: **M, 1–3h**

Improve structured generation for the app-flow target:

1. Weight mutating operations toward add.
2. Keep reset, backspace, query, and add-again present but not dominant.
3. Favor Telex triggers, vowels, uppercase forms, and known placement-sensitive families.
4. Preserve uniform fallback across all ASCII alphabetic input.
5. Add short named seeds for each spec rule and edge family.

Do not over-tune the corpus to only happy-path Vietnamese syllables. Include ugly but valid ASCII sequences.

Success criteria:

- Fuzzing reaches more Telex-specific branches quickly.
- Seeds remain readable and small.
- Random valid ASCII streams still occur.

---

### Stage 4 — Add conservative metamorphic checks

Effort: **M–L, 3h–1d**

Add public-only equivalence properties:

1. Reset equivalence.
2. Query insertion equivalence.
3. Backspace-to-empty/fresh equivalence.
4. Narrow case-pair checks only where the spec is unambiguous.
5. Pass-through behavior under effective-full.

Prefer two independent public states over inspecting internals.

Success criteria:

- Properties compare observable behavior, not private fields.
- Failures minimize to clear public operation histories.
- No property depends on a full reimplementation of Telex composition.

---

### Stage 5 — Consider semantic validators

Effort: **M–L**

After the exact codepoint table is trusted, consider:

1. Tone-category validation.
2. At-most-one non-level tone in the active current word.
3. Possibly stricter Vietnamese syllable-shape checks only if the engine contract actually promises them.

Be conservative. A fuzz harness should not reject valid-but-weird input merely because it is not a natural Vietnamese syllable.

Success criteria:

- The validator is independent.
- Its scope is the active composed word, not arbitrary visible text across resets.
- The property is documented as a public semantic guarantee, not a linguistic assumption.

---

### Stage 6 — Defer internal and negative fuzzing

Effort: **L if ever needed**

Add internal `State` fuzzing only if public fuzzing is insufficient. Add negative tests only for guard behavior that is meant to be supported.

Do not spend early effort here.

## Main risks and mitigations

- **False positives from invalid preconditions:** keep mirroring the app contract; never add past full or backspace past empty.
- **False positives from over-semantic validation:** avoid full Telex reference logic; use exact output sets and metamorphic equivalence first.
- **Overfitting to known examples:** weight Telex-relevant inputs but preserve broad ASCII exploration.
- **Slow/flaky normal tests:** isolate long runs in a separate target and keep corpus seeds minimal.
- **Brittle tests tied to internals:** defer `State` fuzzing; prefer public ABI observations.
- **Weak oracle despite more fuzzing:** exact allowed codepoint validation should happen before spending much effort on larger input space.
- **Corpus bloat:** keep only minimized reproducers and one seed per meaningful scenario.

Bottom line: first make the oracle stricter, then add a full-buffer target, then improve generation, then add carefully scoped metamorphic checks. Do not add negative fuzzing or internal-state fuzzing yet.
